name: Kerry Pippin
history: An Irish early dessert apple on record since 1802 and known in England by 1819. Hogg credited its wider spread to Robertson, a Kilkenny nurseryman who died in 1839, and ranked it among the finest early dessert apples.

look.description: Small, neat oval fruit with a glossy pale yellow skin, streaked and flushed bright red on the sunny side, sometimes with a trace of fine russet.

taste.summary: Hard, very crisp yellowish flesh with a brisk, sugary and aromatic flavour of the sub-acid type. Older writers found it very juicy, while the National Fruit Collection describes it as rather dry. Best eaten soon after picking.

tree.notes: A hardy, medium-sized tree that 19th-century growers recommended for dwarfing stocks, bush forms and espaliers. Cropping was described as good by Hogg and moderate by Bunyard.

pollination.notes: Flowers early: the National Fruit Collection records full bloom in the first week of May, so group 2 is inferred. Assume it needs an early-to-mid flowering partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates like Ireland and western Britain, where it has long been grown.
climate.poor_climates: No record of use in hot regions; an early, small dessert apple like this would likely ripen soft and colour poorly in warm summers.

grow_notes: A good choice for a small garden tree or trained form in Ireland or western Britain. Pick at the end of August and eat within a few weeks, and plant an early-flowering partner nearby.

name: Ballyfatten
history: A cooking apple from Northern Ireland, first recorded in 1802; it shares its name with a townland in County Tyrone. It is kept in the National Fruit Collection, but little has been written about it.

look.description: Tall, ribbed, conical fruit, pale greenish-yellow, with a mottled pinkish to red-brown flush and a little russet.

taste.summary: Firm, white, fairly dry flesh with a plainly acid flavour, suited to cooking rather than eating fresh.
taste.best_eaten: Cooking apple; keeping season not recorded

tree.notes: Recorded as a tip-bearer, so prune lightly and avoid shortening every shoot; better as a standard or bush than a spur-trained form.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom in mid to late May, later than most varieties, so group 5 is inferred. Pair it with another late-flowering apple.

climate.best_climates: Cool, wet maritime climates like Ulster where it originated; its late bloom helps it avoid spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance in hot or continental climates; values are inferred from its Irish origin.

grow_notes: A heritage cooker for Irish or northern British gardens, worth planting where late frosts are common. Because it fruits at the shoot tips, prune by renewal rather than hard spur pruning.

name: Duke of Devonshire

origin.place: Holker Hall, Cartmel, Lancashire (now Cumbria), England
origin.parentage: Unknown; often thought to be related to Ashmead's Kernel because of its similar look and flavour
origin.raised_by: Mr Wilson, gardener to the Duke of Devonshire

history: Raised in 1835 by Wilson, gardener on the Duke of Devonshire's Holker Hall estate in north Lancashire, and introduced around 1875. Edward Bunyard considered it essential as a very late dessert apple, and it has stayed a favourite with russet enthusiasts.

look.description: Small to medium, roundish-oval fruit, dull golden-yellow with a faint brownish-red cheek and a heavy net of russet; the stalk is very short and thick.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained, rather dry cream flesh tinged green. The flavour is concentrated and boiled-sweet fruity, with a rich nutty finish. Sweet-sharp in the manner of Ashmead's Kernel rather than the sweeter Egremont Russet; it needs time in store and is best from about December into March.
taste.best_eaten: Feb-Apr, after several months in store

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and a regular cropper that makes a good standard. Young trees can show variegation in leaves, wood and fruit.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records mid-season bloom (full flower around 11 May), so group 3 is inferred. Any mid-season diploid will pollinate it.

climate.best_climates: Cool, wet northern and western Britain, where its good scab resistance pays off; it was raised on the Cumbrian coast.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot climates; a late russet like this is likely to lose acidity and keeping quality where summers are hot.

health.other: Reported as very resistant to scab and generally healthy, like most russets.

grow_notes: One of the best late russets for wet northern gardens. Leave the fruit on the tree into October, store it cool, and plan to eat it from February onwards.

name: Sops in Wine
history: An old English apple named for its red-stained flesh, which looks as if it had been soaked in wine. Hogg called it very ancient, but the name was used loosely for several red-fleshed apples, so the identity is uncertain; the National Fruit Collection holds accessions that ripen a month apart.

look.description: Roundish, slightly ribbed fruit almost entirely covered in a dark crimson flush, near-black on the sunny side and under a whitish bloom; the flesh is stained red.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy flesh streaked red, sweet but not especially rich; some writers call it pleasant, others almost flavourless, and Hogg noted a faint cider-like astringency. Valued more for its colour than its taste.

tree.notes: A vigorous, spreading, very hardy tree that crops freely and regularly; Hogg noted that it was free of canker.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection accessions bloom early (late April to early May), so group 2 is inferred; Orange Pippin lists group 3. Pair it with an early or mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate England, especially the South West, where old red-fleshed apples of this name were grown.
climate.poor_climates: No evidence of use in warm regions; heat would be expected to reduce the dark skin colour and staining of the flesh.

health.other: Shows some resistance to canker and some susceptibility to scab.

grow_notes: A curiosity for a heritage or cider orchard, grown mainly for its red-stained flesh. It needs room to spread and crops readily. Buy from a source that names its accession, because more than one apple goes by this name.
